stories.headline: Michigan Democrat confirms sister-in-law's terror watchlist lawsuit days before Obama campaign appearance
stories.note: El-Sayed admitted on camera that his sister-in-law sued over being on the terror watchlist, a fresh headache days before Obama campaigns with him.
body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, confirmed Saturday night that his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, was a plaintiff in a 2016 federal lawsuit challenging her alleged placement on the government's terrorist watchlist.
Fox News senior correspondent Mike Tobin put the court documents to El-Sayed directly and asked whether she had been on the list. El-Sayed answered with a simple "Yeah."

He then defended her, saying she "did nothing wrong," and turned his fire on Republican opponent Mike Rogers, blaming a screening system he said people like Rogers built. The 2016 complaint says she faced extra airport screening starting in 2012 and was believed to be off the list by 2016.

El-Sayed claimed she sued and won, but the record is murkier: a federal appeals court reversed a ruling for the plaintiffs in 2021, and a separate damages suit was tossed in 2017. The FBI told Fox it never confirms or denies who is on the watchlist, and the lawsuit itself doesn't show wrongdoing by Jukaku or El-Sayed.

Why it matters: Barack Obama is set to rally with El-Sayed on Oct. 24, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, and this lands on top of separate claims about his family's alleged Muslim Brotherhood ties, which his campaign calls racist and false. Rogers called those allegations "disqualifying," and the story keeps the pressure on Democrats in a must-win Senate seat.

stories.headline: Top takeaways from JD Vance town hall: Costly gas, DC corruption, immigration hot takes and the war
stories.note: Vance went into a CBS town hall in battleground Michigan, blamed Biden-era refinery losses for gas prices, and hit Democrat El-Sayed over his synagogue-attack remarks.
body: Vice President JD Vance took questions from Michigan voters at a CBS News town hall in Flat Rock, weeks before midterms that could decide control of the Senate. Michigan's open seat pits Republican Mike Rogers against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

Asked first about high gas prices, Vance pointed to Iran's attacks on shipping and to refining capacity lost under Joe Biden, saying about 20% of U.S. refining went offline then. He said the administration is using the Defense Production Act to rebuild it, though that will take time. Anchor Tony Dokoupil pushed back that Trump and Vance have been in office almost two years.

On corruption, Vance said he sees no evidence of it from the president or the administration, called selling White House access "disgusting and despicable," and said he would comply with congressional subpoenas if Democrats win Congress. On immigration, he admitted some of his H-1B rhetoric was imperfect but said his target is companies that replace American workers, not the visa holders themselves.

On Iran, Vance argued the U.S. has already destroyed Tehran's nuclear program and is now seeking a verifiable long-term commitment, adding that gas would cost far more without the Navy guarding the Strait of Hormuz. Asked by a Democratic father whose kids survived the Temple Israel attack to condemn antisemitism, Vance did so, then criticized El-Sayed's "hurt people hurt people" remark. El-Sayed had condemned the attack and later apologized for his wording.

Why it matters: Vance went onto a mainstream network's turf in a key swing state, stayed on message on energy, immigration and Iran, and tied the Democratic Senate nominee to one of his most damaging moments.

stories.headline: House panel warns Singham-linked nonprofits: Comply with subpoenas or face Congress
stories.note: House Republicans are threatening sworn depositions for leaders of three Singham-funded left-wing groups, and possibly Singham himself, over suspected CCP influence.
body: The Republican-led House Ways and Means Committee has stepped up its investigation into three nonprofits tied to Shanghai-based Marxist tech mogul Neville Roy Singham, warning they must hand over subpoenaed records by Tuesday or their leaders could be questioned under oath.

The letters went to The People's Forum in New York, the left-wing outlet BreakThrough News, and the Massachusetts think tank Tricontinental. Fox News Digital sources say 21 people, including Singham, are on the committee's list for possible depositions. The panel hasn't announced that any deposition subpoenas have actually gone out.

Chairman Jason Smith of Missouri said the groups are trying to hide where the money goes, warning that "their leaders will answer the Committee's questions under oath" if documents aren't produced. The committee says money moved through shell companies and donor-advised funds in ways that can obscure foreign-linked sources. Fox previously traced about $40.3 million from Singham to these three groups.

The groups say the probe targets their political views and First Amendment rights, and their lawyers called it a "witch-hunt." Singham is also under a federal grand jury investigation in Manhattan over possible financial crimes, though no charges have been announced.

Why it matters: Republicans are pressing a high-profile case about Chinese Communist Party influence flowing into American activist and media groups on the left, and they're showing they'll use subpoena power to get answers before the midterms.

stories.headline: Mamdani praised over move to dismantle controversial NYC industry — but insiders say there's more to the story
stories.note: NYC carriage drivers say socialist Mayor Mamdani's horse-carriage ban will wipe out family livelihoods and $400,000 medallions with no reimbursement.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Council Speaker Julie Menin announced a deal this week to phase out Central Park's horse-drawn carriages, with a council vote expected next week on a bill that would end the rides starting in June 2028.

The push picked up steam after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan died from a fall in June, and the bill now bears his name. Animal-rights activists have long accused the industry of mistreating horses, pointing to viral videos of collapses and runaways.

Carriage owner Frank Riccobono told Fox News Digital the 168-year-old tradition is being unfairly targeted. He paid nearly $400,000 for his medallion and said, "there's no reimbursement in this bill." His wife said losing the business would put the family's home and table at risk.

Mamdani says the city has a duty not to leave the roughly 200 drivers "out to dry," and Menin's office says it's forming a working group with the transit workers' union. But union shop steward Christina Hansen said drivers haven't heard from Mamdani directly and worry rescues can't afford to care for the retired horses.
Why it matters: It's a clear example of a socialist mayor's agenda landing on working families and small-business owners, with union workers saying City Hall isn't listening to them.

stories.headline: 'Moderate' AG's office turned to groups that spent years suing prisons for recruiting help, emails reveal
stories.note: Emails show Arizona's Democratic AG Kris Mayes's top deputy asked the ACLU and a prison-litigation group for hiring help, undercutting her 'moderate' law-and-order pitch.
body: Internal emails obtained by Fox News Digital show that Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes's chief deputy, Daniel Barr, repeatedly asked the ACLU and the Berkeley-based Prison Law Office to recommend lawyers for state corrections work, including candidates for the corrections department's top legal job.

Barr already had deep ties to both groups. Before joining Mayes's office, he spent years at Perkins Coie litigating alongside them against Arizona's prison system in a case where a judge found conditions unconstitutional. In one 2023 email he wrote, "Still no takers for the ADCRR general counsel job," asking the groups for suggestions.

Both groups push to cut incarceration sharply, and the ACLU has published pieces backing defunding the police. Fox found an ACLU staffer floated one candidate who was already suing the corrections department in civil rights cases. The emails don't show what other help, if any, the groups gave, and the person ultimately hired had no ties to either group.

Mayes's campaign said the ACLU has sued Mayes repeatedly and pointed to her record of backing police and seizing 27 million fentanyl pills. Barr, the AG's office, the ACLU and the PLO didn't respond to Fox.

Why it matters: Mayes won in 2022 by just 280 votes and faces Republican state Sen. Warren Petersen in November. This gives the GOP an opening to argue her office's actual hiring doesn't match her tough-on-crime branding.

stories.headline: Becoming a lawyer could get cheaper and faster under looming Trump admin shakeup
stories.note: The Trump administration may soon strip the ABA's accrediting arm of federal recognition, which could open cheaper, faster, less DEI-driven routes to becoming a lawyer.
body: The Trump administration is expected to decide by late December whether to pull federal recognition from the American Bar Association's law school accrediting arm. Education Department staff have already recommended denying renewal, citing more than 26 compliance problems, and the call now rests with Under Secretary Nicholas Kent.

Losing recognition wouldn't automatically end ABA accreditation or change state bar rules, but experts told Fox it could speed up states' moves toward alternatives. Texas and Florida have already ended exclusive reliance on the ABA, and Ohio, Tennessee, Alabama and Washington are moving in that direction.

Adam Biggs of the University of Austin, which is planning a tuition-free law school outside the ABA system, said the ABA forces a costly "one size fits all elitist model" that saddles grads with debt and leaves rural areas short of lawyers. The Justice Department has also warned the ABA over rules limiting adjunct professors, saying they raise tuition.

Experts said most students wouldn't lose federal loans, since their schools are covered by a parent university's accreditation; Sarah Parshall Perry estimated about 15 standalone law schools could face trouble. The ABA disputes the department's findings, and it already voted in September to repeal its diversity standard.
Why it matters: It's a conservative win against an entrenched, left-leaning gatekeeper, and it promises lower costs and more choices for future lawyers.
